abstract: Tetrameric and pseudo-tetrameric cationic channels, which are targeted by many drugs and toxins, play key roles in the cell physiology and pathophysiology. This diverse superfamily of P-loop channels includes but is not limited to voltage-gated potassium, sodium and calcium channels, TRP channels, and ionotropic glutamate receptors. In hundreds of crystal and cryoEM structures of P-loop channels, the general folding is rather similar but subfamily-specific structural details vary greatly. The latter underlie atomic mechanisms of ion selectivity, gating, sensitivity to drugs and toxins, and dysfunction of thousands disease-associated variants. Understanding these mechanisms may benefit from comparative analyses of multiple structures. Here, we propose a statistical method to reveal structural determinants of folding in related proteins, which involves clustering of residue-residue contact energies. We applied the method to a pH-gated potassium channel KcsA and a voltage-gated sodium channel NavAb. Twenty 3D-aligned experimental structures of each channel with universal residue labels were downloaded from database www.plic3da.com and Monte Carlo energy minimized. Residue contact energies clustered in the multidimensional space of contacts automatically discriminated open vs. closed states of KcsA, and wild-type vs. chimeric structures of NavAb. We found and analyzed specific contacts that underlie structural peculiarities. The proposed approach may help detecting folding peculiarities and their structural determinants between subfamilies of P-loop channels, within individual subfamilies, and could be adapted to other proteins.
